title: The Educated Barbarian: Meditations analysis (part. 13)
summary: Part 13 of NH's reading of Marcus Aurelius' Meditations. He covers refusing to pass on negativity, the ruling faculty, stepping back from trouble, stripping objects of their glamour, applying philosophy rather than just talking about it, and self-respect as the source of freedom. He ties these ideas to bodybuilding, which he values more for the discipline and mindset it builds than for the muscles.
claims: Apes have a strong sense of fairness: a monkey refuses cucumber when its neighbour gets fruit
The best revenge is not to copy the person who wronged you; the stoic ends the cycle of transmitted negative energy
First step: feel the anger but don't let it dictate action; the enlightened step is to not feel the insult at all
People who act badly want you to act the same; staying righteous makes them feel worse
The ruling, thinking part of you is the real you; once you grasp that, the body is a vessel you can turn into whatever you want
Evolution is not random; it is a perfect method of selection
Whether God exists matters less than what belief in order means for your life
When something upsetting happens, step back before reacting unless safety demands it; the issue shrinks and your reaction is what hurts most
Following Musashi: take a long time over small things and deal quickly with big urgent ones, for which you should already be prepared
The more you practise stepping back, the easier it gets; rushing into solutions makes it harder
Strip objects of their glamour: money is paper whose value is social convention, gold is a rock valued for rarity
Take care of yourself first; the most effective charitable people are strong and well fed
Objects exist for their function: use the car, wear clothes until they break; you are never a slave to the object
Denying physical property also denies ownership of your own body and mind, which leads to slavery
Talking about concepts without applying them is mental masturbation; reading stoicism without applying it fails stoicism
The muscles die with you, but the energy, discipline and mindset built training them are what make it worthwhile
What bodybuilding made of his brain and willpower is 15 times more valuable to him than the physique
Pleasures of the flesh and social applause are fleeting; learning, crafting and developing a passion are what matter
Blaming society, fate or genetics keeps you weak; you always have free will to react
When he prays he doesn't ask for things; he gives thanks for being free and able to provide for himself
